name: Renal arteries
func: Carry oxygen-rich blood from the aorta to each kidney. About a fifth of everything the heart pumps goes through them, so the kidneys can filter the blood and keep salt, water and blood pressure balanced.

levels.kid:
Your kidneys are like two coffee-bean-shaped cleaning machines in your back. To clean your blood, they need blood to arrive! The **renal arteries** are two big tubes, one for each kidney, that bring blood straight from the biggest tube in your body, the **aorta**.

Even though your kidneys are small, they get a LOT of blood, about one out of every five squirts from your heart. That's because they have to wash all of your blood many times every day.

Inside the kidney, the renal artery splits into smaller and smaller branches, like a tree, until the tiniest ones reach millions of tiny filters. The filters keep the good stuff and send the waste out as pee.
levels.hs:
The **renal arteries** are paired branches of the **abdominal aorta**. They leave the sides of the aorta at roughly the level of the first and second lumbar vertebrae (**L1–L2**), just below where the **superior mesenteric artery** branches off the front of the aorta.

The **right renal artery** is longer, because the aorta sits slightly to the left of the midline. It runs **behind the inferior vena cava** to reach the right kidney. The **left renal artery** is shorter and runs behind the left renal vein.

Each artery enters the kidney at the **hilum**, the notch on its inner edge, usually lying between the renal vein in front and the **renal pelvis** (the start of the ureter) behind. A handy front-to-back order at the hilum is **vein, artery, pelvis (VAP)**.

The kidneys receive about **20–25% of cardiac output**, roughly 1 litre of blood per minute at rest, even though together they weigh only about 300 grams. That huge flow isn't for oxygen; it's so the kidneys can filter about 180 litres of plasma every day and keep blood volume, salt, acid and blood pressure under control.
levels.college:
Within or just outside the hilum each renal artery usually divides into an **anterior and a posterior division**, which give rise to **segmental arteries** (classically five: superior, anterosuperior, anteroinferior, inferior and posterior). Segmental arteries are **end arteries**: they do not anastomose, so blocking one causes a wedge-shaped **infarct** of that renal segment. This is the basis of surgical **segmental (partial) nephrectomy**.

The branching then runs: segmental → **interlobar** (between the renal pyramids) → **arcuate** (arching along the corticomedullary junction) → **cortical radiate (interlobular)** arteries → **afferent arterioles** → the **glomerular capillary** tuft → **efferent arterioles** → peritubular capillaries and, from juxtamedullary nephrons, the **vasa recta**. Two capillary beds in series is unusual and is what lets the kidney both filter and reabsorb.

Each renal artery also sends small branches to the **adrenal gland** (inferior suprarenal artery) and the **ureter**.

**Variants are common**: about a quarter to a third of people have **accessory (polar) renal arteries**, extra vessels running directly from the aorta to a kidney pole. A lower-pole accessory artery can cross and compress the ureter. These remnants reflect the kidney's embryological "ascent" from the pelvis, during which it picks up successive arterial supplies from the aorta.

Sympathetic nerves travel along the artery from the **renal plexus**.
levels.phd:
Renal blood flow is tightly **autoregulated**: across a mean arterial pressure of roughly 80–180 mmHg, glomerular filtration rate stays nearly constant. Two mechanisms do this. The **myogenic response**: stretch of afferent arteriolar smooth muscle opens stretch-sensitive cation channels, depolarises the cell, opens L-type calcium channels and causes constriction. **Tubuloglomerular feedback**: the **macula densa** cells of the thick ascending limb sense luminal chloride via the **NKCC2** cotransporter; more chloride delivery triggers release of **ATP/adenosine**, which constricts the afferent arteriole through A1 receptors.

The **juxtaglomerular (granular) cells** in the afferent arteriole wall are modified smooth muscle cells that store and release **renin**. Renin release rises with low afferent stretch (intrarenal baroreceptor), low macula densa sodium chloride (via prostaglandins), and **β1-adrenergic** sympathetic input. Renin cleaves angiotensinogen to angiotensin I; ACE (largely in lung endothelium) makes **angiotensin II**, which preferentially constricts the **efferent** arteriole, maintaining glomerular pressure when perfusion falls. This is why drugs that block angiotensin II can drop GFR sharply when both renal arteries are narrowed.

**Prostaglandins** (PGE2, PGI2) dilate the afferent arteriole and protect flow in low-volume states, explaining why NSAIDs can tip vulnerable kidneys into injury.

The medulla receives only about 10% of renal flow through the slow-moving **vasa recta**, preserving the medullary osmotic gradient by **countercurrent exchange** but leaving the outer medulla (thick ascending limb, S3 segment) chronically near-hypoxic. Medullary oxygen tension sits far below cortical levels, which is why these segments are first hit in ischaemic **acute tubular injury**.

Current research focuses on **renal denervation** for resistant hypertension and on imaging the microcirculation with contrast-enhanced ultrasound and BOLD MRI.
levels.expert:
The headline disease is **renal artery stenosis**. The two main causes look different:
- **Atherosclerotic** stenosis: older patients with vascular disease, narrowing at the **ostium** (origin) or proximal third of the artery.
- **Fibromuscular dysplasia (FMD)**: classically younger patients, affecting the **mid-to-distal** artery with a **"string of beads"** appearance on angiography.

Stenosis lowers pressure beyond it, the juxtaglomerular cells sense under-perfusion and pour out renin, and the result is **renovascular hypertension**. Clues on exam and history: hypertension that starts suddenly, is resistant to three or more agents, or worsens abruptly; an **abdominal (epigastric) bruit**, especially one that continues into diastole; **flash pulmonary oedema**; asymmetric kidney sizes on ultrasound; and a sharp rise in creatinine after starting an ACE inhibitor or ARB.

**Imaging**: duplex Doppler ultrasound (raised peak systolic velocity, abnormal resistive index), **CT angiography** or **MR angiography**, with catheter **digital subtraction angiography** as the reference standard. Treatment in general terms: blood pressure and cardiovascular risk control for atherosclerotic disease, and **balloon angioplasty** (usually without stent) for FMD.

Other emergencies: **renal artery embolism** (often from atrial fibrillation) presents with sudden flank pain, blood in the urine and a high LDH; CT shows a wedge-shaped non-enhancing area. **Renal artery dissection** and **traumatic intimal injury** occur in deceleration trauma.

**Surgical relevance**: accessory renal arteries must be mapped before **living donor nephrectomy**, aortic aneurysm repair and partial nephrectomy, because cutting one infarcts its segment. In **endovascular aneurysm repair (EVAR)**, the stent graft's "neck" is planned around the lowest renal artery.

keyPoints: Paired branches of the abdominal aorta at about L1–L2
Right renal artery is longer and passes behind the IVC
Segmental arteries are end arteries: a blockage causes a wedge infarct

test.explain: The aorta lies a little left of midline, so the right renal artery must travel further, passing behind the inferior vena cava.

test.q: What fraction of cardiac output do the kidneys receive at rest?
test.explain: Roughly a fifth to a quarter of cardiac output, around 1 L/min, flows to the kidneys so they can filter plasma.

test.q: The renin-releasing cells in the afferent arteriole wall are the ______ cells.
test.explain: Juxtaglomerular (granular) cells are modified smooth muscle cells that sense stretch and release renin.

test.q: A young patient's angiogram shows a 'string of beads' in the mid renal artery. Most likely cause?
test.explain: FMD affects the mid-to-distal artery in younger people, while atherosclerosis narrows the ostium in older patients.

test.q: Because segmental renal arteries don't connect with each other, they are called ______ arteries.
test.explain: End arteries have no collaterals, so blocking one infarcts a wedge of kidney.
